findings_addressed.what_changed: SystemModeService.readCache/writeCache and TenantResolverService.readCache/writeCache now fail open: a Redis error is treated as a cache miss and the caller falls through to the control-plane query instead of rejecting. fix.summary:
All five findings fixed and covered by tests; unit suite 443/443 green, `npx tsc --noEmit -p apps/api/tsconfig.json` clean (the only errors are two pre-existing ones in apps/api/src/billing/stripe-real.driver.ts, a file another agent is mid-edit on), prettier and eslint clean on every file I touched.

Three mechanisms, not three symptoms:

1. Fail-open caching. `SystemModeService` and `TenantResolverService` now treat a Redis error as a cache miss and fall through to the control plane, and `SystemModeService.bust()` no longer rejects the admin write that opens/ends a mode window. New `SystemModeService.resolveGlobalSafe()` cannot throw at all — it degrades to the last successfully-resolved global mode, then to NORMAL_MODE — and it is what the middleware's ALWAYS_PASS branch and the public /system-mode/current endpoint call. A dead Redis (or a dead Redis AND a dead control DB) can no longer 500 /healthz, /readyz, /metrics or the /admin/system-mode recovery lever. A new `FailOpenMemo` (exported from redis.service.ts, 5s TTL, capped) stops the fail-open path turning one dead Redis into a control-DB query per request; the healthy path is byte-for-byte unchanged.

2. Cold Redis clients in jobs. `JobContext` now carries a connected `redis`; `startScheduledJobs` accepts the looser `JobRunnerContext` and owns one long-lived client when the caller doesn't supply one (closed in `stop()`, never closing a borrowed one). `registry.ts` passes ctx through, and both offending jobs use `ctx.redis`/`ctx.emails` and `await redis.ready()` before their first command. `RedisService.ready()` waits for the ioredis 'ready' event, rejects on 'end', times out at 10s, and deliberately does not reject on 'error' (ioredis emits one per reconnect attempt, and retryStrategy always retries). worker.ts is outside my file list, so it does not yet hand over its `sharedRedis` — the runner's own client makes the fix correct today, and the handover is a one-line change reported separately.

3. Runner lying about outcomes. `toScheduledJobResult()` (exported, pure, unit-tested) sets ok:false when any of `tenantsFailed` / `failed` / `stillFailing` is non-zero, appends the failure to the message, and keeps the handler's counts — which the worker's /healthz already serializes, so no worker.ts change is needed for the health surface. Partially-failed runs log via console.warn. I also fixed the empty-reason log line the audit saw (`accrual failed for tenant=reltwo: `) with a `describeError()` helper used by the runner and all five tenant sweeps.

I deliberately did NOT make `TenantResolverService.invalidate()` fail open — that call is what stops a suspended or relocated tenant being served from cache (TEN-03/TEN-04), so the caller must learn it failed. There is a test pinning that decision.

So a tenant where EVERY reservation fails to expire still returns tenantsFailed:0 and the runner records ok:true with 'N tenant(s) scanned'. That is precisely the failure shape reliability-07 describes ("holds silently stop expiring"), just at row granularity instead of tenant granularity. Also unfixed and explicitly requested by the finding: libriant_worker_job_last_ok / libriant_worker_job_tenants_failed do not exist (worker.ts:110-135 still exposes only uptime + in-flight), and worker /healthz still returns HTTP 200 even when every lastResults row is ok:false — so nothing alerts on it without a body-parsing probe.

verdicts.reasoning: Verified by reading stripe-retry.job.ts directly. `const redis = ctx?.redis ?? new RedisService()` at line 68, and `await redis.ready()` at line 83 is the first statement inside the try — strictly before `new PlatformSettingsService(redis)`, before the driver/BillingService construction, and before the sweep-lock `redis.client.set(lockKey,'1','EX',300,'NX')` at line 98 that the audit reproduced as the abort point. verdicts.bypass: None found. One behavioural side effect worth knowing: `stillFailing` is now a FAILURE_COUNT_KEY, so a single permanently-poisoned webhook row will pin this job at ok:false on every 5-minute tick indefinitely once billing is enabled.

regressions.issue: New fail-open points the wrong way and hides a real outage. `resolveEffective({tenantId}).catch(() => this.modes.resolveGlobalSafe())` means that when the control DB errors while resolving the TENANT-scoped event, the endpoint the web app polls reports the GLOBAL mode — normally 'normal'. A tenant deliberately placed in maintenance/out_of_order therefore silently loses its takeover page for the duration of any control-DB blip. This directly contradicts the rule the same commit writes into SystemModeService.lastKnownGlobal ("falling straight back to normal there would flip the takeover page off mid-maintenance, which is the opposite of what the operator asked for"). No test covers this path. The correct degradation is the tenant's last known mode, or pickStricter(lastKnown, global) — not silently the laxer global one.

reliability-07's masking defect survives at row granularity. The per-reservation catch inside expireOneTenant only logs a warn; no counter is bumped and nothing reaches the tenant-level catch, so a tenant in which every single reservation expiry throws still contributes tenantsFailed:0. toScheduledJobResult() then records ok:true with the message 'N tenant(s) scanned; nothing to expire'. Holds stop expiring and /healthz still reports the job healthy — the exact harm the finding describes.

`this.lastKnownGlobal = resolved` is only assigned on the cache-MISS path; resolveGlobal() returns early at line 64 on a cache hit without touching it. In a multi-process deployment one process can keep hitting a key another process refreshes, so its lastKnownGlobal can stay arbitrarily stale (not the ~30s the TTL implies). That stale value is exactly what resolveGlobalSafe() serves when Redis and the control DB are both down — the scenario it exists for. Assigning it on the cache-hit path too costs nothing.

Including 'stillFailing' and 'failed' in FAILURE_COUNT_KEYS makes two jobs latch permanently red rather than flag a transient problem: one poisoned stripe_webhook_events row keeps stripe-webhook-retry at ok:false every 5 minutes forever, and one unpurgeable artifact keeps export-file-cleanup at ok:false hourly (export-cleanup.job.ts:87). With no metric and no alert rule yet this is only noise, but the moment an alert is built on lastResults.ok it will be a permanently-firing one, which reintroduces the alarm fatigue the finding is about.

The deliberate fail-CLOSED decision on TenantResolverService.invalidate() (now pinned by a new test: 'a stale suspended tenant is not safe') is bypassed by a second code path that reaches the same sink. The hard-delete handler builds the resolver keys itself and does `await this.redis.client.del(...resolverKeys).catch(() => {})`, swallowing the very failure invalidate() is written to surface — so a Redis error during tenant deletion leaves the slug resolving to a dropped database for up to the cache TTL, silently. Pre-existing rather than introduced, but the new test asserts an invariant the codebase does not actually hold.

verify.overall:
All five findings hold up under adversarial reading: in every case the guard is placed before the dangerous operation, the sink the audit named is actually covered in the diff, and the new tests are mutation-sensitive rather than tautological (I traced each one to a specific assertion that breaks if the fix is removed). `npx tsc --noEmit -p apps/api/tsconfig.json` is clean — cleaner than the report claimed, the two stripe-real.driver.ts errors are gone — and `vitest run --project unit` is 58 files / 448 tests green.

The strongest refutation is scope, not correctness. The report's summary asserts that "the Stripe/apply webhooks can no longer be turned into 500s by an unreachable Redis"; that is demonstrably false. `apps/api/src/billing/stripe-webhook.controller.ts:90` issues a bare `redis.client.set(...,'NX')` with no try/catch on a path that is in ALWAYS_PASS, so the middleware now waves the request through into an unguarded Redis command. Same for line 120's DEL in the error branch. `/apply` is fine (its limiter fails open), so only the Stripe half of that sentence is wrong — but it is wrong about an endpoint the finding itself enumerates.

Beyond the two files the implementer honestly flags as another agent's (effective-plan, platform-settings), two more unguarded request-path caches go unmentioned anywhere in the report: `announcements/announcement-delivery.service.ts:71/136` and `catalog/isbn.service.ts:52/63`. Net effect for reliability-02: `/healthz`, `/readyz`, `/metrics`, `/system-mode/*`, `/admin/system-mode/*`, login, and — importantly — loan checkout/return all survive a Redis outage now, but plan-gated reads such as `GET /t/:slug/reservations` still 500, so the audit's acceptance criterion "reads still serve" is only half met.

For reliability-07 the runner-level lie is genuinely gone and the counts now reach /healthz, but the same lie persists one level down at `reservation-expiry.job.ts:202`, where per-reservation failures are swallowed with no counter at all — a tenant whose every hold fails to expire still reports `tenantsFailed: 0, ok: true`. That is the finding's own harm statement ("holds silently stop expiring"), unmitigated.

The one change I would push back on rather than merely note is `public-system-mode.controller.ts:41`. Swallowing a failed tenant-scoped resolve and answering with the global mode makes a deliberately-declared tenant maintenance window vanish from the endpoint the web app polls, which is the exact failure direction the same commit argues against three files away. It is untested and should degrade to the tenant's last known mode instead.

## The defect and the fix

One bug, two finding ids. `unlimitedPlan()` substitutes `UNLIMITED_INT = Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` for every int feature while billing is off; `StorageService.put` multiplied `max_storage_mb` by 1024² and bound the product into the reservation `UPDATE`. Confirmed the arithmetic independently: `BigInt(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER) * 1024n * 1024n` = 9444732965739289378816, which is 1023× `2^63 - 1`, hence SQLSTATE 22003 on every upload.

Belt and braces, as asked, but placed where I own the code:

1. **Drop the predicate** (primary). `apps/api/src/plans/effective-plan.service.ts` now exports `UNLIMITED_INT` and a new `isUnlimitedInt(limit)` predicate (`>=`, not `===`, so anything at or above the sentinel reads as "no ceiling"). `StorageService.put` asks that question and, when the answer is yes, runs the reservation `UPDATE` **without** the `AND "storageUsedBytes" + $n <= $ceiling` clause — nothing out of range is bound because nothing is bound at all.
2. **Clamp the conversion** (secondary). New module-private `quotaCeilingBytes(limitMb)` in `storage.service.ts` floors at 0, truncates, and clamps the byte product at `9223372036854775807n`. Today only the sentinel can get that big (`plan_feature_values.valueInt` and `tenant_plan_overrides.valueInt` are int4, whose max 2147483647 MB = 2251799812636672 bytes, comfortably inside int8), so this is pure defence against a future wider column or a new sentinel.

I did **not** clamp `UNLIMITED_INT` itself (the finding's alternative). `apps/api/src/plans/effective-plan.service.spec.ts:244,250` asserts the value is exactly `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`, and that file is outside my ownership list — clamping the constant without updating those two assertions would leave the unit suite red. Clamping at the byte-conversion site is arguably the better layer anyway: int8 is a storage-column concern, not a plan concern. Reported the spec path in `out_of_scope_files_needed` in case you want the constant clamped as well.

One behaviour change worth flagging: on the unlimited path, `reserved === 0` can no longer mean "doesn't fit", only "the tenant row is gone" (a stale resolver cache). It now throws `NotFoundException('Library not found.')` rather than a 402 claiming a storage limit that does not exist.

## The test configuration (what changed and why)

`apps/api/test/integration/setup.ts` no longer does `process.env.BILLING_ENABLED ||= 'true'` for the whole suite. The launch default (false) is now what every integration file runs under.

I audited which specs actually depend on enforcement being on, rather than assuming:

- **`import-api.spec.ts` — genuinely needs it.** Line 111 asserts `bulk_import_enabled` is `false` and the route answers 402. With billing off, `unlimitedPlan()` opens the gate.
- `import-engine.spec.ts` — does **not**. Its quota test stubs `getLimit` directly.
- `import-worker-e2e.spec.ts` — does **not**. It creates a `bulk_import_enabled` override; works either way.
- `desktop-access.spec.ts` — does **not**. It branches on `res.body.billingEnabled`.
- `admin-audit.spec.ts`, `admin-role-guard.spec.ts`, `cross-tenant-isolation.spec.ts`, `library-workflow.spec.ts`, `scheduled-jobs.spec.ts` — no plan-gate assertions.

So exactly one file needs the old value. **Because I don't own `import-api.spec.ts`, the opt-in lives in `setup.ts` as a one-entry named allowlist** (`NEEDS_BILLING_ENFORCEMENT`), keyed on `basename(expect.getState().testPath)`. I verified empirically that `expect.getState().testPath` is populated in a Vitest setup file, and that top-level `await` in a setup file completes before the spec module is imported — both checked with a throwaway project against this repo's own Vitest 4.1.11. **The proper end state is a `process.env.BILLING_ENABLED = 'true'` line at the top of `import-api.spec.ts` and the allowlist deleted from setup.ts**; that is a two-line change for whoever owns that file.

**Second setup.ts change, and this one is load-bearing rather than cosmetic.** `PlatformSettingsService` caches the resolved switch in Redis for 30 s under a *single global key*, and the suite shares one Redis. `admin-role-guard.spec.ts:90-107` documents the resulting cross-file poisoning — measured at "import-api.spec.ts getting 201 instead of 402 roughly one run in ten" back when every file at least *agreed* on the env value. fix.summary:
Established a real trust boundary for "who is the client", and gave signup an admission control that does not depend on that claim.

(a) `clientIp()` (apps/api/src/platform/client-ip.ts) now honours `X-Real-IP` ONLY when the immediate TCP peer is a trusted proxy, validated with `node:net` BlockList; an untrusted peer gets its own socket address, headers ignored. Default trust set is loopback + private/link-local (exactly the compose topology — the API is only ever reached from the Caddy container), narrowable via `TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS`, which throws at boot if malformed. main.ts replaces `app.set('trust proxy', true)` with the same predicate, closing the second spoof vector (`req.ip` = leftmost X-Forwarded-For). infra/caddy/Caddyfile gains a `(cloudflare_only)` snippet (a `remote_ip` matcher over Cloudflare's published v4+v6 ranges plus `private_ranges`, then `respond 403`) imported as the first directive inside every `route` that proxies to api:3001 — app host, admin host and the marketing site's `/apply` — so `header_up X-Real-IP {CF-Connecting-IP}` can never run for a non-Cloudflare peer. scripts/prod-bootstrap.sh gains a `--firewall-only` host mode that builds a LIBRIANT-ORIGIN chain in DOCKER-USER (not ufw — Docker's DNAT sits ahead of ufw's INPUT chain, which is why the documented `ufw allow` would never have worked) for 80/tcp and 443/tcp+udp in both iptables and ip6tables.

(b) AdminAuthService keys its lockout on (adminId, clientIp) in Redis the way LoginService does, and no longer writes `status`/`lockedUntil` from unauthenticated input — the amplification that let five requests 403 a live admin cookie is gone. `recordSuccess` still writes `status:'active'` solely to heal rows the old code locked.

(c) Signup gains a hard global cap on concurrent provisioning (a Redis sorted-set concurrency gate, cap 4, stale-swept at 120s) acquired after DTO validation and released in `finally`. It rejects with 429 (a 4xx passes the exception filter verbatim; 503 would have been re-skinned as a support-code 500). No email dependency — EMAIL_DRIVER is console. The AUTH-05 advisory global bucket is unchanged and its rationale preserved.

Caddy directive ordering across handle/handle_path/route could not be validated here (no caddy/docker binary), so the guard deliberately uses the pattern this Caddyfile already proves in production: a matcher + `respond` inside a `route`, which honours source order.

Verified: 448/448 unit tests pass, `tsc --noEmit` clean, prettier clean, `sh -n` clean on the bootstrap script. Integration tests were not run (need DB/Redis); loopback peers normalise to 127.0.0.1 and stay trusted, so supertest flows that set X-Real-IP are unaffected.

verify.overall:
Package is roughly half-landed, and the half that landed is not the half the report says is load-bearing.

What is genuinely good: the Caddyfile is VALID — I built caddy 2.8.4 with the local Go toolchain and `caddy adapt --config infra/caddy/Caddyfile` exits 0 with the `not remote_ip …` + `respond 403` pair emitted first inside each protected subroute, so the implementer's blocking concern about directive ordering is resolved in their favour. `npx tsc --noEmit -p apps/api/tsconfig.json` is clean and the unit suite is 449/449. The admin DB-status write is genuinely eradicated (no remaining writer of `'locked'` anywhere in apps/api or packages), which kills the worst part of authn-authz-03. client-ip.spec.ts tests real invariants, not the implementation.

Why I still refuse all four:

1. The app-side trust boundary is inert in the production topology. The API publishes no host port, so its only peer is Caddy — always trusted — and Caddy stamps X-Real-IP from whatever CF-Connecting-IP arrived. The entire control is the Caddy remote_ip matcher, not client-ip.ts. docs/deployment-hetzner.md claims the reverse ("a forged CF-Connecting-IP is worthless once the app checks its peer"), which is the one sentence most likely to get the edge guard removed by a future maintainer.

2. That single control has a hole: the allowlist ends in `private_ranges`. No compose network enables IPv6, so the caddy container is v4-only while Docker publishes 443 on `[::]` (RUNBOOK.md:1153 says so), which forces userland docker-proxy to relay v6 connections and rewrite the source to the bridge gateway — a private address, therefore allowlisted. The origin's IPv6 address is in the repo and the runbook instructs proxied AAAA records to it. That restores authn-authz-01, input-and-files-02 and, through them, input-and-files-03 in full, and `--firewall-only` cannot close it because docker-proxy terminates on INPUT while LIBRIANT-ORIGIN hangs off DOCKER-USER. Suggested remedy: publish as `0.0.0.0:80:80` / `0.0.0.0:443:443` so no `[::]` listener exists, and re-check with `nmap -6`.

3. authn-authz-03's admin sign-in DoS is fully intact in shipped code — the controller never passes the ip, so every lock lands in one global `…:unknown` bucket, and verify() checks the lock before the password so the real admin cannot clear it. The seven new tests all pass an ip that production never supplies; they are green against a code path nobody can reach. This is a three-token fix at admin-auth.controller.ts:85/105/114 and should not ship without it.

4. input-and-files-03's gate is well built but caps concurrency, not volume: ~3.6 permanent tenant databases per second still gets through, so the finding's stated impact is throttled rather than bounded, and the Lua that enforces the cap is never executed by a test (eval is mocked to a constant).

Recommend: not accepted. Required before re-review — thread the ip through admin-auth.controller.ts; remove the [::] publish (or otherwise make a v6 peer distinguishable from the health-check peer); guard `/webhooks/*`; correct RUNBOOK §3.2c; and re-run the three original executed probes (rotating X-Real-IP against /auth/login and /auth/signup, and the five-request admin lockout) against a booted stack over BOTH address families.

findings_addressed.what_changed:
Replaced the buffer-everything reader with a streaming one and made every writer streaming too.

READS: readTables() (one `SELECT * FROM "t"` per table into a JS array, all tables retained in `out`) is gone. withTableReader() now opens ONE `BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ, READ ONLY` per database (pg_dump's own form — the tables are now read minutes apart, so a shared snapshot is what stops a loan referencing a copy the copies file never contained), reads each table's shape from a zero-row describe, and readTableInBatches() pulls rows through a server-side cursor with `DECLARE ... NO SCROLL CURSOR` / `FETCH FORWARD 5000` / `CLOSE`. No new dependency: raw cursor SQL through the pg client already in the image, so pg-cursor / pg-copy-streams were not needed.

PRE-FLIGHT: assertExportSizeSane() sums `GREATEST(reltuples,0)` from pg_class before a single row is read and refuses there. The old MAX_EXPORT_ROWS check ran after the table was already materialised.

THE CAP ITSELF: raised 2,000,000 -> 25,000,000 and demoted to a runaway backstop. The old value was the second half of the finding — an Institutional library (400k books / 520k copies / 100k members / 2M loans / 3M audit ≈ 6M rows) could never export its own data, which is what GDPR Art. 20 portability rests on here. Memory no longer scales with rows, so the cap is now only a sanity bound (~4x the largest plan) and is still enforced cumulatively mid-stream by createRowStreamer as a backstop for never-analysed tables where reltuples is unknown.

WRITERS: JSON is assembled on the wire byte-identically to the old `JSON.stringify(all, null, 2)`; CSV writes header + one row at a time; both go through a new BufferedWriter (64 KB write-behind, honours stream backpressure, and captures 'error' so an ENOSPC on the shared volume fails the job instead of killing the worker with an unlistened error event). XLSX uses ExcelJS.stream.xlsx.WorkbookWriter with useSharedStrings:false and a per-row commit() instead of buildWorkbook().

SECOND OOM FOUND AND FIXED: streaming the reads was NOT enough for xlsx. ExcelJS hands every committed row to the sheet's zip stream and never honours the backpressure that comes back (its StreamBuf.write is documented as never returning false), so the un-deflated sheet XML queues in front of zlib — MEASURED 47 MB of live Buffers per 100k rows (arrayBuffers grew linearly and survived a forced GC), i.e. ~1.4 GB for one 3M-row audit_log: the same OOM, off-heap. writeXlsxSheets now waits per batch (awaitZipDrain) until that queue is under 32 MB, with a 5 s per-batch budget so it can never park. The internals-dependent lookup is exported as xlsxSheetQueueBytes and pinned by a test so it cannot silently become a no-op.

ZIP PATH: csv/json/xlsx now spool to `${jobId}-*` temp files and hand archiver the path — the idiom the sql path already used and which generate()'s finally already cleans up on both paths. Deliberately not a live PassThrough into the archive: a stalled entry would leave the writer awaiting a 'drain' that never comes and wedge the single-slot export queue (EXP-002).
findings_addressed.residual_risk:
1. NO LIVE POSTGRES was reachable in this environment (5432 and 6432 refused, no docker), so the new SQL (DECLARE/FETCH/CLOSE, `BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ, READ ONLY`, the pg_class/reltuples pre-flight) was never executed against a real server. The batching logic is proven against a fake client; the SQL forms are standard but unexecuted. An integration test is the gap — see out_of_scope_files_needed.
2. The REPEATABLE READ snapshot is held for the whole per-database read (same as pg_dump), which holds back vacuum on that tenant DB for the export's duration.
3. Zip spooling costs transient disk (roughly the uncompressed export) and, for scope=all, the spools of all tenants accumulate until finalize — unchanged from how the sql format already behaved, and a large improvement on holding it in RAM. Deleting each spool on archiver's 'entry' event would remove even that.
4. reltuples is an estimate; a never-analysed table reports -1 and contributes 0, which is why the cumulative backstop is kept.
5. 25,000,000 is a judgement call, not a measured limit.

fix.summary:
performance-01 is fixed, and a second OOM of the same shape was found and fixed on the way.

WHAT NOW BOUNDS PEAK MEMORY (the brief's question, answered explicitly):
1. Reads — one FETCH_BATCH_ROWS (5,000) batch, from a server-side cursor. Nothing accumulates across batches or across tables; `out.push(...)` of whole tables is gone.
2. CSV/JSON — a 64 KB write-behind buffer that honours stream backpressure. Peak = one batch of row objects + 64 KB.
3. XLSX — ExcelJS streaming writer (no shared strings, row-level commit) plus a 32 MB cap on the un-deflated XML queued in front of the zip.
4. Zip — every artifact is spooled to a temp file and archiver is given the path, so a scope=all export holds no tenant's rows in RAM.
5. Nothing is read at all if the pg_class pre-flight says the database is over the limit.

MEASURED (harness at /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-leontgmusic-Projects-libriant/17d734a8-b1ae-4f54-aee8-56a4167eb571/scratchpad/mem-harness.ts, which drives the real writers with audit_log-shaped rows; ~100 MB process baseline):
- Streamed CSV peak RSS: 225 MB @ 250k rows, 288 MB @ 1M, 282 MB @ 3M — flat over a 12x row range, producing 524 MB of output.
- Streamed JSON peak RSS: 298 / 296 / 288 MB over the same range (884 MB of output at 3M).
- Old buffered shape, same rows: 384 MB @ 250k, 1030 MB @ 1M, 2191 MB @ 3M — linear, and at 3M it cannot even finish: `RangeError: Invalid string length`, so the old CSV path was doomed on a real Institutional library even with infinite RAM.
- XLSX before the zip throttle: 501 MB @ 500k, 737 MB @ 1M, 1165 MB @ 2M (heapUsed flat at ~145 MB — the growth was live off-heap Buffers, confirmed by forced GC). After: 375 MB @ 500k, 391 MB @ 2M, 312 MB @ 3M, with no wall-clock regression (11.9 s vs 12.8 s at 2M).

The 1 GB worker (WORKER_MEM_LIMIT) is now comfortable for the numbers the Institutional plan sells, and the 2M-row cap that made that plan unable to export its own data is raised to 25M as a runaway backstop only.

Verification of the tests themselves: mutating the loop terminator from `< batchSize` to `<= batchSize` (the classic silent-truncation bug) fails 8 of the 23 new tests, including the JSON byte-equality, the CSV row count and the xlsx read-back. Full unit suite 449/449 green, `tsc --noEmit` clean for src/export, prettier and eslint clean. Only apps/api/src/export/** was touched.

verdicts.reasoning:
The mechanism is gone, not just the symptom, and I verified it independently rather than trusting the report.

DIFF CONFIRMS THE CLAIM. `readTables()` and its `out.push({name, columns, rows, ...})` accumulator are deleted; `buildWorkbook()`/`tablesToObject()`/`toCsv()` (all whole-table-in-RAM) are gone. Reads now go through `readTableInBatches` (DECLARE NO SCROLL CURSOR / FETCH FORWARD 5000 / CLOSE) inside one `BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ, READ ONLY` per DB. `assertExportSizeSane()` is the FIRST statement executed inside that transaction, before the pg_tables listing and before any describe or FETCH — the audit's 'check after the dangerous operation' is genuinely inverted (export-processors.ts:576-580).

NO SECOND PATH TO THE OLD SINK. Every non-sql format reaches rows only via `withTableReader` -> `createRowStreamer` -> `readTableInBatches`; `produceSingleFile` (json/xlsx) and `addTargetToArchive` (csv/json/xlsx) both funnel through it, so the pre-flight cannot be skirted by choosing a format or a scope. `dumpSql` never buffers (pg_dump --file). `grep` finds no other caller of the removed helpers anywhere in apps/ or packages/.

I EXECUTED THE SQL THE IMPLEMENTER COULD NOT. Their #1 residual risk ("no live Postgres was reachable") is discharged: /opt/homebrew has postgresql@16, so I stood up a throwaway cluster on 127.0.0.1:55432, seeded a tenant-shaped DB and drove the REAL exported functions against it. Results: `BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ, READ ONLY` accepted; `assertExportSizeSane` returned est=12347 and threw ExportTooLargeError at maxRows=100 after one catalog query; audit_log 12,345 rows in 3 batches = 12,345 read (no drop/dup); empty table -> 0 batches; the double-quote table name `we"ird` quoted correctly; the same cursor name re-DECLAREd for the next table and for a full re-read (so CLOSE really works); `SET LOCAL statement_timeout=300` + a slow FETCH cancelled at the FETCH, proving the timeout is now per-FETCH not per-whole-table; the cumulative row backstop tripped mid-stream at 10,000.

I MEASURED MEMORY WITH THE REAL DRIVER, NOT A FAKE. 500k real rows (98 MB table) through the real writers from the real cursor: CSV 79 MB out / 1.7 s / peak RSS 264 MB; JSON 153 MB out / 2.0 s / 267 MB; XLSX 20 MB out / 3.8 s / 418 MB — against a ~100 MB tsx baseline, i.e. flat, versus the audit's 1,443 MB RSS on one table.

I ALSO RE-DERIVED THE XLSX CLAIM RATHER THAN BELIEVING IT. Independently reproduced the ExcelJS zip queue: 40k committed rows leave 12.6 MB queued in `ws.stream.pipes[0]`, so the off-heap growth is real and `xlsxSheetQueueBytes` finds it. Ran 10 sheets x 200k rows through a replica of `awaitZipDrain`: peak RSS 359 MB, flat across sheets, 0 batches hit the 5 s give-up. The throttle works, including for sheets 2..N (I specifically checked whether a later sheet's stream is unpiped-and-therefore-invisible while an earlier zip entry drains — it is piped, pipes.length===1, so it does not fail open there).

BYTE-COMPATIBILITY IS REAL, NOT ASSERTED. I rebuilt the OLD `JSON.stringify(tablesToObject(data),null,2)` and old `toCsv()` from git HEAD and diffed them against the new streaming writers on a hostile row (nested object+array, Date, Buffer, null, undefined, numeric-string '-42', formula-injection '=cmd|calc', embedded quote/comma/newline/unicode, plus an empty table) at batchSize=1 and flushBytes=7 so every batch and flush boundary is crossed: byte-identical for both. XLSX fidelity: `useStyles:false` does NOT lose date formatting — the new file still carries s="1" with numFmt mm-dd-yy, identical to the old workbook (I unzipped and compared sheet1.xml); strings move from shared-strings to t="str", which round-trips.

OFF-BY-ONE: `if (res.rows.length < batchSize) break` is correct at both boundaries (12@5 -> [5,5,2] in 3 fetches; 10@5 -> [5,5] plus one empty fetch that never reaches onBatch), and both `est > maxRows` and `totalRows > maxRows` are strict, so exactly-at-limit passes. Verified against the real cursor, not just the fake.

NOT TAUTOLOGICAL: the xlsx queue-pin test drives real ExcelJS and would fail if the internals lookup returned null. `npx tsc --noEmit -p apps/api/tsconfig.json` clean; `vitest run --project unit` 449/449 green. I edited nothing.
verdicts.bypass:
The bound is a ROW count, not a byte budget, so the "memory no longer scales with data" claim has a hole a tenant controls. FETCH_BATCH_ROWS is fixed at 5,000 regardless of row width, and the tenant schema has unbounded columns: packages/db-tenant/prisma/schema.prisma has `description String?` on Book and `customFields Json @default("{}")` on Book/Copy/Member/Loan (and the control DB has stripe_webhook_events.payloadjson). A library whose customFields/description average 200 KB puts ~1 GB of row objects in one batch and OOMs the 1 GB worker exactly as before — and assertExportSizeSane cannot see it, because reltuples counts rows and this DB may hold only a few hundred thousand of them, far under 25,000,000. The JSON writer then makes a second copy per row (normalizeRow + JSON.stringify). A byte-aware batch (shrink batchSize from the previous batch's measured size, or FETCH by a bytes budget) would close it.

Two softer ones, both narrower: (1) `awaitZipDrain` is best-effort, not a cap — after XLSX_DRAIN_BUDGET_MS (5 s) it returns with the queue still over 32 MB, so on a CPU-starved worker where deflate level 9 cannot keep up the xlsx queue grows unbounded again, just slower; nothing in the suite would notice, because XLSX_QUEUE_BYTES/XLSX_DRAIN_BUDGET_MS are not exported and no test measures xlsx memory — mutating XLSX_QUEUE_BYTES to Infinity leaves all 449 tests green. (2) `xlsxSheetQueueBytes` returning null makes awaitZipDrain a no-op by design; the pin test catches an ExcelJS upgrade at CI time but nothing catches it at runtime.

regressions.issue: STALE_RUN_MS is 1h keyed on createdAt (not startedAt) and its comment still says "far longer than any healthy export" — a claim this change invalidates. Raising MAX_EXPORT_ROWS 2,000,000 -> 25,000,000 deliberately sanctions runs an order of magnitude longer, and the export worker is concurrency:1 (export-worker.ts:41), so a job can sit queued for most of the hour behind another export and be reaped minutes into its own run. When it fires, sweepExpiredExports calls purgeJobArtifacts(jobId), which deletes everything matching `${jobId}-*` and `${jobId}.*` (export-processors.ts:196) — and this change is exactly what made csv/json/xlsx spool to `${jobId}-*` temp files (previously only sql did). So the sweep now unlinks a LIVE export's spools and its output file out from under archiver and marks the row failed; the job then either dies on ENOENT during finalize() or "completes" and writes back filePath pointing at a deleted inode. Not observed firing at current throughput (500k real rows streamed in 1.7-3.8s locally, so 25M is minutes not hours), which is why this is medium and not high — but the guard's stated safety margin is no longer true and it deletes files belonging to running work.

New unguarded disk pressure on the volume shared with tenant uploads. csv/json/xlsx now spool the full UNCOMPRESSED artifact to ${STORAGE_ROOT}/_exports/${jobId}-* before archiver reads it, and generate() only deletes the spools after finalize() — so for scope=all every tenant's spool accumulates simultaneously. Measured on a real DB: 500k audit-shaped rows = 79 MB CSV / 153 MB JSON, so one 6M-row Institutional library is ~1 GB (csv) to ~1.8 GB (json) of spool plus the zip, and N tenants multiply it. STORAGE_ROOT is /srv/libriant/storage, the same docker volume mounted into api and worker for tenant file uploads (infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml:52,217,288); nothing checks free space before spooling, and the per-tenant storageUsedBytes quota in storage.service.ts does not cover _exports. The old failure mode was a worker OOM (bad, isolated to the worker); the new one is ENOSPC on a volume every tenant writes to. The implementer's own residual note #3 suggests the fix: delete each spool on archiver's 'entry' event instead of at finalize.

The REPEATABLE READ READ ONLY transaction is now held open for the entire per-database read (minutes) with no idle_in_transaction_session_timeout set anywhere in the repo, where the old code used one implicit transaction per SELECT. This holds back vacuum/HOT-pruning on that tenant DB and pins a backend for the export's duration. Disclosed by the implementer (residual #2) and it buys a real correctness property (cross-table snapshot consistency), so it is a deliberate trade rather than an oversight — recording it because nothing in the repo bounds it.

assertExportSizeSane sums reltuples over every relkind='r' in schema public, including _prisma_migrations, which the export itself excludes (the pg_tables query filters it out). Verified live: est came back 12,347 for a DB whose exported tables hold 12,347 rows only because _prisma_migrations reported -1 and clamped to 0. Harmless over-count today, but the pre-flight and the thing it gates are counting different sets of tables. Same run also confirmed the documented reltuples caveat is live: a never-analysed table with 100 real rows contributed 0 to the estimate.

Test-strength gap rather than a code defect: the suite pins that the zip-queue signal is still DISCOVERABLE (xlsxSheetQueueBytes non-null and >100 KB) but never that the throttle built on it ENGAGES. XLSX_QUEUE_BYTES and XLSX_DRAIN_BUDGET_MS are module-private and no test measures xlsx memory or drain behaviour, so setting XLSX_QUEUE_BYTES to Infinity — reverting the second OOM fix entirely — leaves all 449 tests green. The CSV counterpart ('memory in flight does not grow with the row count') does assert the real invariant via maxChunk; xlsx has no equivalent.

verify.overall:
performance-01 survives adversarial review: actually fixed, and the verification is stronger than what the implementer was able to run.

I did not take the report on trust. I read the diff, confirmed readTables/buildWorkbook/tablesToObject/toCsv are deleted with no surviving caller anywhere in the monorepo, and confirmed the pre-flight is the first statement executed against the DB rather than a rename of the old post-hoc cap. Then I closed the implementer's own blocking gap: they reported "NO LIVE POSTGRES was reachable, so the DECLARE/FETCH/CLOSE, the REPEATABLE READ READ ONLY transaction and the reltuples pre-flight are unexecuted." A Homebrew postgresql@16 is installed on this machine, so I stood up a throwaway cluster, seeded a tenant-shaped DB, and ran the real exported functions against it. Every unexecuted SQL form now has an execution behind it: the BEGIN form is accepted, the cursor loop reads 12,345 rows in 3 batches with no drop or duplicate, an empty table produces zero onBatch calls, a table named we"ird is quoted correctly, the cursor name is reusable across tables and across a full re-read, statement_timeout now fires per FETCH rather than per whole-table SELECT, the pg_class pre-flight refuses before reading, and the cumulative backstop trips mid-stream. I also measured memory with the real pg driver rather than a fake: 500k real rows produce 264/267/418 MB peak RSS for csv/json/xlsx against a ~100 MB baseline, versus the 1,443 MB the audit measured on a single table.

Two claims I specifically tried to break and could not. Byte-compatibility: I reconstructed the old JSON and CSV writers from git HEAD and diffed them against the new streaming ones on a hostile row (nested object/array, Date, Buffer, null, undefined, numeric string, formula-injection payload, embedded quote/comma/newline/unicode, plus an empty table) at batchSize=1 and flushBytes=7 so every batch and flush boundary is crossed — byte-identical both times. The xlsx zip throttle: I reproduced the off-heap queue independently (12.6 MB after 40k committed rows), checked the fail-open I expected on sheets 2..N (a later sheet's stream is piped immediately, so the null path does not trigger), and ran 10 sheets x 200k rows through a replica — flat at 359 MB peak with zero batches hitting the 5 s give-up.

The one hole worth acting on before release is not the one the implementer flagged. Their residual list worries about unexecuted SQL (now discharged) and about 25,000,000 being a judgement call. The actual weak point is that the batch bound is a row count, not a byte budget: FETCH_BATCH_ROWS is 5,000 regardless of row width, and the tenant schema has unbounded `description` and `customFields Json` columns, so a library with fat custom fields can put ~1 GB in one batch and OOM the same 1 GB worker — with reltuples-based pre-flight blind to it, because that DB may hold only a few hundred thousand rows. That is the same failure the finding describes, reachable through the new code, and it deserves a byte-aware batch size.

Beyond that, two medium regressions are worth queueing rather than blocking on: the 1h stale-export reaper keys on createdAt and deletes ${jobId}-* files, which this change turned into live spool files for csv/json/xlsx while also sanctioning much longer runs; and those spools now land uncompressed on the storage volume shared with tenant uploads with no free-space check, converting a worker-local OOM into a cross-tenant ENOSPC. tsc is clean, the unit suite is 449/449, and I made no edits to the repo.
